scope: 89 candidate INSTANCE prompts / 16 MAIN proposals separately held
reviewer_instruction: Do NOT open the Stage B crosswalk, author package, solution, D-band, QRT operation or predicted W before freezing your independent Stage A record. Derive science, assumptions, units, limits, counterexample, primary operation and five-factor evidence independently. Record unavailable diagrams as HOLD. A blind packet does not appoint a reviewer.

items.prompt: A thermometer repeats 40.8, 40.8 and 40.9 in a 40.0 °C reference and 70.8, 70.9 and 70.8 in a 70.0 °C reference. The user concludes it is accurate to 0.1 °C for any temperature. Evaluate the evidence and design a discriminating check.
A sensor reads 2 at 10 °C, 62 at 90 °C, and 32 in a specimen. A 50 °C check reads 33. Select a correction model and report what the specimen data actually justify.
Sensor X maps raw −5 to 15 over −20 to 60 °C; Y maps raw 0 to 80 over the same temperatures. X reads 5 and Y reads 35. Put both results on a single Celsius axis and compare.

A calibrated instrument reads 15 units at 0 °C and 95 units at 40 °C. A reserved 20 °C check reads 58 units exactly. A sample moves from readout 35 to 75. Test the proposed affine model, calculate conditional temperature change and explain whether the absolute endpoints are validated.

Two metal blocks at identical temperature have masses 1 kg and 4 kg; a third block at constant higher temperature receives 10 W continuously. A claim says the first two must contain equal energy and the third cannot exchange heat. Supply counterexamples and state what needs to be checked before inferring zero net accumulation.

An unheated object matches the surroundings at 20 °C; a hotter electronically warmed solid loses 26 W and receives 26 W; an ice-water mixture receives 15 W while remaining at its melting point. Compare their energy diagrams and identify which are genuine equilibrium or steady-state examples.

A heated cylindrical model has input power per unit length K X²/r² and lateral loss per unit length H r at a fixed temperature. A redesigned surface has radius 2r and doubles H, with K unchanged. Find the required factor change in X and identify the assumption needed for the prediction.

Two 1-hour simulated cooling trials hold a room at constant temperature. Known load rates are4 and7 kW; common unknown leakage L is added. Electrical rates are2 and3 kW. Fit COP and L; predict a 2-hour run at known load5.5 kW, then compare measured electrical energy5 kWh and compute rejected energy if model fits.

A virtual heating unit requires 24000 J, draws 160 W and loses 40 W. Its ideal conductor model is changed to twice the length and 3/2 the diameter at the same applied voltage. Compute the new resistance ratio, useful rate and time, compare with the original time, and check the energy budget.

Two rods of metal and wood have been in one room for hours. A warm hand touches each; metal feels colder. Later the rods connect the same warm and cold reservoirs. Explain why the two observations need not contradict equal initial temperatures, and identify a measurement of each claim.

At fixed ΔT=20 K a nominal 4 K/W slab with an unknown extra path loses 7 W. Model A uses a changed effective slab resistance proportional to thickness. Model B retains nominal R with a fixed bypass. Doubling thickness gives 4.5 W. Test both, infer the bypass if supported, then predict total loss when thickness is quadrupled.

Hot face 50 °C, cold face 20 °C. Sequential layers R=1 then 5 K/W, and a separate 15 K/W bridge. Construct a labelled path diagram and temperature profile on the layered branch; calculate total power.

Tank A has warm lower fluid density 990 and cool upper fluid density 1000 kg/m³. Tank B has a warm salty lower layer density 1010 and a cool upper layer density 1000. Predict which arrangement develops buoyancy-driven mixing, describe return flow, and explain why equal heating labels are insufficient.

A student observes that a covered warm vessel cools more slowly than an uncovered one and concludes the lid eliminates convection entirely. Critique this conclusion and propose observations or controls separating internal fluid circulation, evaporation and heat transfer to the surroundings.

Three identical dry warm plates at matched temperature require 18 W (still air, warm face upward), 10 W (still air, warm face downward) and 28 W (downward face with fan) to hold steady. Flow tracing shows upward plumes in the first and forced airflow in the third. Compare net losses and assess the convection models; what cannot be inferred from powers alone?

Two shores receive equal solar power. Shore X has lower effective thermal capacity and warms faster despite similar absorption. Near-surface air above X warms more than above Y; background wind is negligible. Explain a possible circulation and why equal irradiation does not imply equal surface temperature. Identify when the inference could fail.

A dry plate is independently measured to have C=300 J/K. At the same initial temperature its warming rates are 0.08 and 0.16 K/s for incident powers 90 and 150 W. A third trial at 120 W gives 0.10 K/s. Assume α and loss fixed across trials. Infer parameters from first two trials, test the third and explain whether a unique physical model survives.

Plate A absorbs 75 W, loses 15 W and has C=600 J/K. B absorbs 50 W, loses 10 W and has unknown C. Find the capacity threshold below which B initially warms faster, and predict the result for C=300 J/K. What assumption limits the comparison?

A thermal-imaging model reports two panels at equal temperature and geometry. Panel X has higher measured infrared radiance than Y in the sensor band. A student claims X is visibly brighter and necessarily cools faster. Assess both claims and propose a test that separates emissivity from other energy-loss paths.
One sample freezes in a cooling bath while a second pure solid at the bath temperature shows a flat trace. Explain the different energy pathways and identify an observation that distinguishes them.
Equal masses melt in 40 s and 75 s. The first has input 25 W and loss 10 W, the second input 12 W and loss 4 W. Evaluate a claim that the longer transition necessarily has greater energy requirement.

An initially all-liquid pure sample at its freezing point loses net energy at 18 W for 50 s until fully solid. It then cools for 25 s. Construct temperature and solid-fraction graphs and compare energy leaving in the two intervals.

A damp and a dry plate at matched temperature are exposed to a fan. Both require extra heater power, but the wet plate's mass also decreases. Explain the separate energy pathways, and propose a comparison that distinguishes them.

At same surface temperature and area, dry/wet powers are 9/14 W in one enclosure and 15/25 W in another. Measured true evaporation is 0.002 and 0.003 g/s; supplied L_v=2500 J/g. Assess both trials and design an additional measurement to discriminate the unexplained difference.
A damp surface receives 30 W and has other loss 10 W. At evaporation rates 0.006 and 0.010 g/s, L_v=2500 J/g, determine which tends to warm and which cools, then find the balancing rate.

A pure sample and a dry plate have identical flat traces while both heaters operate. A student concludes both must be melting. Construct compatible distinct histories and identify observations to discriminate.
At same initial temperature, powers 45 and 75 W give slopes 0.10 and 0.22 K/s. At 60 W an unused trial gives 0.19 K/s. Infer C and loss, and assess whether one common pair explains all exact data.
A 300 J/K unchanged-phase sample begins at 25 °C. Net powers are +30 W for 20 s, −15 W for 20 s and zero for 10 s. Draw both histories and calculate energy for each interval and final T.

A thermal simulator requires 18000 J. Independent input measurements give A=120 W and B=90 W. A alone takes180 s, B alone takes 18000/70 s. Model X assumes common fixed loss for all trials; model Y allows another loss only when both inputs operate. Joint trial takes 100 s. Fit and test X and Y, then predict an unused joint trial at total input190 W if joint loss stays unchanged.

Two identical positive-expansion rods are heated equally. One is fixed at its left end, the other at its centre. Explain how the right-end displacements compare and why neither measurement by itself proves different material expansion.

A freely heated bonded strip bends. A technician claims the curvature alone gives the ratio of the layers' thermal expansion coefficients. Explain why different layer stiffnesses or thicknesses could yield different curvature for the same coefficients; propose a discriminating experiment.

Two rods extend from opposite fixed walls toward a 1.8 mm gap. A is 1.5 m, α=16×10⁻⁶/K; B is 0.8 m, α=20×10⁻⁶/K. A warms by twice B's temperature rise. Find B's rise at first contact and the gap if B warms 20 K.

A full model vessel at4 °C holds1000 g water in1000 cm³. At a warmer state, density .998 g/cm³. Model X assumes unchanged capacity; Y uses independently measured capacity1003 cm³. Compare predicted overflow and test a reserved measured headspace of about .996 cm³. Then suppose a separate cold trial has density .9999 and capacity999.5 cm³; calculate spill mass.

A rigid column area 50 cm² holds 450 g of water and 50 g floating ice; initial density1.000 g/cm³. Final density is measured as0.998 g/cm³ after all ice melts. Compare predicted change with a level sensor reporting +0.200 mm exactly. Check whether evaporation of 1 g would make the level higher or lower than the no-loss prediction.

A and B loss-power estimates are 16±3 W and 20±3 W from matched steady trials. A student claims B definitely loses more and that a second identical reading proves it. Evaluate and design an improved test.
Four matched steady-power trials: A/X=11 W, B/X=17 W, A/Y=15 W, B/Y=19 W. Infer treatment effects at each location, test the additive model and propose a control.
Two vessels have C=150 and300 J/K, start45 °C, and after20 s are41 and42 °C; at40 s they are39 and40 °C. Construct temperature and average loss-power histories; compare total energy lost.
A hot solid C=400 J/K at75 °C enters liquid C=500 and vessel C=100 at15 °C. External loss1200 J. Determine final equilibrium T and audit all energy terms.
Hot-minus-liquid energy residuals are 500 J at vessel rise3 K and 900 J at7 K. A third at5 K gives760 J. Fit first two, test unused run, and determine whether the exact data justify one common model.

A vessel calibration transfers800 J and raises T by8 K. In mixing, vessel and liquid C=300 J/K start25 °C; a 0.1 kg solid starts85 °C; final T=35 °C. A second mixing run with solid at95 °C gives final T=37 °C. Infer c from first run, predict second and assess consistency.

A proposed ordinary cyclic heat engine between reservoirs takes heat from a single hot reservoir and claims 100% conversion to work with no other effect. The developer argues that Q_in=W satisfies conservation. Assess the argument and distinguish energy-balance consistency from physical feasibility.

Water and vessel total C=600 J/K at20 °C receive0.05 kg ice at0 °C. L=300000 J/kg; c_water=4000. Determine state and amount of ice remaining, then find the critical initial warm-body temperature for complete melting at0 °C.

A complete engine cycle absorbs18000 J, rejects12000 J; 75% of rejected heat reaches a vessel with0.02 kg ice at0 °C and negligible vessel capacity. L=300000, c_water=4000. Predict work, efficiency and final state. A separate probe reports final liquid20 °C. Test consistency.

A buzzer inside a chamber remains visibly vibrating as air is removed. An external sensor still detects a small signal. Explain why this does not establish gas-borne sound in vacuum, and propose a discriminating observation.

A reed vibrates at measured 300 Hz and 1 mm amplitude. Microphone reading falls from 10 to 5 after moving a panel. A calibrated check tone at that position falls from 6 to 3 too. Compare panel-path and detector-gain models and choose an additional control.

A membrane's successive maxima at 2,8,14 ms and a microphone's maxima at 3,9,15 ms are recorded. A separately timed onset gives 7 ms propagation. Sketch both traces and reconcile the different apparent offsets.

A calibrated source sensor records positive maxima at0,8,16 ms of amplitude10,8,6 mm. A receiver records peaks at0,8,16 ms of amplitude5,2,1 arbitrary units. Construct both normalized amplitude sequences, infer period and assess whether the receiver's faster fading establishes greater mechanical energy loss at the source.
Three equilibrium positions 0,15,30 mm have displacements −2,+1,+1 mm. A report says the negatively displaced particle marks rarefaction. Explain what the data actually establish about each gap.

Five equilibrium particles spaced 10 mm apart have measured gaps 11,9,8,12 mm. A report gives displacement [0,1,0,−2,0] mm as the only solution. Construct a different compatible profile, identify the missing constraint, and recover the profile if the fourth particle is known at displacement +1 mm.
Five equally spaced equilibrium positions 0,12,24,36,48 mm have ξ=+2,0,−2,0,+2 mm. Draw displacement and actual spacing, then plot qualitative pressure signs on intervals.

A tap on a pipe is detected early by a contact sensor and later by a microphone. Covering the microphone's air inlet reduces the later signal, while the pipe sensor is unchanged. Explain the possible paths and why timing alone is not enough to identify them.

Two pulses arrive at 2 and 6 ms. An intervention lengthens a known solid segment by 4 m at 2000 m/s, but leaves air geometry unchanged. New arrivals are 4 and 6 ms. Assess competing path labels and propose a further test.

Two paths connect a transmitter and sensor. Route X crosses 0.9 m at 300 m/s and 3 m at 1500 m/s. Route Y is a 4 m solid path at 2000 m/s. Construct a labelled time diagram with segment transitions and arrival order.

The third and tenth peaks of a fixed microphone signal occur at 5 and 19 ms. At one instant the second and eighth matching compressions are at 0.40 and 4.36 m. Infer T, f, λ and v; decide whether 320–340 m/s is consistent.

A sinusoidal trace shows consecutive zero crossings separated by 0.8 ms. Two spatial compressions separated by 0.544 m are visible but the intervening region is missing. A report gives f=1250 Hz and λ=0.544 m. Challenge or defend the report, and specify what observation makes speed unique.

Successive upward zero crossings on a time trace are at 0.5 and 2.5 ms. A spatial snapshot has successive downward zero crossings at 0.30 and 0.98 m. Draw a complete sinusoidal cycle for each with extrema and crossing slopes labelled; determine T, f, λ and v.

Two tones of frequencies150 Hz and twice that frequency have wavelength difference1.1 m. Infer common speed and both wavelengths. A third tone of period4 ms has observed wavelength1.32 m. Check all observations; state what is conditional if media differ.

A pulse arrives after 5.5 ms at 1.05 m and 9.5 ms at 2.45 m using one apparatus. A third distance of 3.50 m gives 12.5 ms. Find speed and offset and decide whether the readings support the fixed-delay model.

A steady source of 400 Hz sends sound across a 0.9 m section with λ=0.75 m followed by 0.6 m with λ=1.25 m. Sketch cumulative travel time versus path distance at all three boundaries and infer overall speed.

A 2 m direct path contains unknown length x in medium A and the rest in B. A 500 Hz source has λA=0.60 m and λB=1.00 m. The apparatus reports 7.2 ms through the mixed path and 5.6 ms through 2 m entirely in B. Both have the same unknown delay. A separate 1 m path entirely in A reports 4.933 ms (rounded). Find x and delay, and assess consistency.

A gas at 289 K gives timings 7 and12 ms for lengths 1.7 and3.4 m. At 400 K lengths 2 and4 m give 7 and12 ms. A third path6 m at400 K reports17 ms. Test a common v²/T and common delay model versus constant speed with adjustable delay, using the reserved path.

A displacement trace for tone A has twice the displacement amplitude of tone B but half its frequency. Both are progressive linear waves. The medium for each is not specified. A report claims IA>IB and A must sound louder. Decide whether the evidence proves either claim; use I∝ρv(fA_displacement)² and construct two compatible impedance cases with opposite intensity order.

At 2 m and 4 m from a source, a calibrated pressure sensor reports peak amplitudes 8 and 4 Pa. At 8 m it reports 1 Pa. Test ideal isotropic lossless spreading in one medium and infer what the data do and do not establish.

Trace A repeats an upward zero crossing every 4 ms and has peak-to-peak pressure 6 Pa. Trace B has successive pressure maxima 2 ms apart and peak-to-peak 3 Pa. Draw one full cycle of each on common scales; compare pitch and intensity in the same medium.

A sinusoidal displacement wave with λ=0.90 m produces the same spatial profile at times separated by 5 ms. A report concludes the material has travelled at 180 m/s. A separate instrument bounds propagation speed to 150–400 m/s. Reject or defend the report and identify every compatible signed propagation velocity.

A periodic pressure wave has λ=1.00 m. At 5 ms a second snapshot has its maxima displaced +0.25 m modulo λ. The speed lies from 100 to 450 m/s inclusive, direction unknown. At 2 ms the maxima have moved +0.30 m modulo λ. Recover signed velocity and justify uniqueness.

A left-moving periodic sinusoidal displacement pattern with λ=0.40 m, amplitude 2 mm and initial trough x=0.10 m has speed 300 m/s. Construct two profiles on 0≤x≤0.80 m separated by 1 ms; identify the later value at x=0.10 m.

A calibrated pressure detector records R=[−2,4,0,1,−3] Pa over five 2 ms bins. Source A alone gives [1,2,−1,0,−2] Pa under matched linear conditions. Reconstruct source B's contribution, draw all three traces, and predict resultant if B's polarity reverses while A is unchanged.
Source 2 m and receiver 10 m from a wall have parallel separation 6 m. v=340 m/s. Calculate both path times and assess a 12 ms separation requirement.
Two sensors (one emits) are 6 m apart parallel to a wall at equal unknown distance. Echo delay after direct sound is 10 ms, v=400 m/s. Recover the wall distance and test a proposed 2 m result.

A receiver records direct arrival at 24 ms and reflected at 40 ms after a pulse. v=250 m/s, equal normal wall distances. Draw the time trace and corresponding image-source geometry, infer normal distance.

A hall's late sound becomes weaker after adding absorptive panels, while measured arrival times of two still-detectable returns remain unchanged. Explain the observations and why unchanged timing does not mean the treatment failed.

An untreated hall and a treated hall both show direct arrival at0 and late group at40 ms, but the treated late amplitude is smaller. A student concludes the panels did not reduce reverberation because the timing is the same. Give a counterexample and a more relevant measurement.

Model X has returns at 12 and 48 ms, amplitudes0.8,0.5. Model Y adds a 28 ms return at amplitude0.25. Direct amplitude1. Detector threshold0.4, duration18 ms, required quiet gap6 ms; observed groups 0–30 and48–66 ms. Threshold then drops to0.2 at duration18 ms, yielding one group 0–66 ms. Finally duration drops to4 ms at threshold0.2. Determine which model fits and predict final separate starts, and explain whether the second trace alone proves there are exactly three reflection paths.

A pulse-echo detector reports a reference at 4 m in uniform medium speed1000 m/s after 10 ms. A normal target beyond a 5 m first layer at1000 m/s and a second medium at1500 m/s returns after 24 ms. Same fixed delay. Find target distance.

Known normal reflectors at 6 and18 m return at 11 and27 ms. At 30 m an independent return is44 ms. Fit common speed/delay and assess the exact third observation; give conditional range for a 35 ms return if the first model were used.

Two pulse-echo units A=(0,0), B=(8,0) m share known speed1500 m/s and common unknown delay. A known 3 m reflector returns at6 ms. The same stationary unknown target returns at 10 ms from both A and B. A third calibrated unit C=(0,6) records a return at approximately7.508 ms with same delay. Determine the target candidates from A/B, then use C to select and verify the location.

A wind instrument plays a higher note when a hole is opened. Its microphone amplitude decreases. Explain how effective vibrating air-column length and radiation/detection can lead to different pitch and amplitude trends.

Two instruments produce spectra with only one detected peak at400 Hz under a narrow-band sensor. A technician concludes they must share the same fundamental and instrument type. Construct two compatible source explanations and specify an improved measurement.

A fixed-end string gives120 Hz. Length becomes 3/4 of original, tension becomes9/4 original and μ fixed. Measured f is240 Hz. Test the ideal model and the length-only explanation; give a further prediction if tension returns to original.

A string wave and radiated airborne tone have common frequency 250 Hz. String speed125 m/s; air speed350 m/s. Two configurations use the same string displacement amplitude but different sounding bodies, with pressure amplitudes 3 and 6 Pa in matched progressive air fields. A student claims the wavelengths are equal and the second configuration is four times as loud. Assess both claims and state a defensible quantitative conclusion.

Only the common second-order arrival at 60 ms is independently identified at v=300 m/s; all other peaks are below threshold. A technician infers the source is centered. Construct two different admissible geometries, show how their first-order predictions differ, and specify a measurement that could establish centeredness.
Source distances 5 and7 m, v=300 m/s. Construct a labelled path table and timing trace through three reflections. Distinguish number of paths from peaks.

An identified first-order echo appears at 16 ms, and the independently identified common second-order peak at 56 ms. Other first return was missed. v=250 m/s. The source/receiver is shifted 1 m right; the new identified first returns are 24 and32 ms. Determine the original wall distances, explain uniqueness, and predict the original missing return and both third-order arrivals.

A pulse is emitted at x=150 m between walls x=0 and300 m. Receiver moves left at30 m/s; speed330 m/s. Determine first four reflection-path arrival times (first and second order), their ordering, and test a detector log showing distinct leading times .833,1.000,1.667,2.000 s. Are all before contact?

v=330 m/s, emitted f_s=330 Hz. Approach frequency440 Hz. Rival models: moving source or moving observer, other stationary. With same speed magnitude reversed, observed recession220 Hz. Infer both speeds and compare predictions.

At v=340 m/s, an ideal open-open tube length0.85 m and a closed-open tube length0.425 m are compared. Draw first two mode families and spectra; explain how equal fundamentals coexist with different higher modes.

v=320 m/s, source f_s=225 Hz approaches stationary resonator at80 m/s. Candidate A open-open length320/600 m; B closed-open length320/1200 m. First response strong. Raise emitted f_s to450 Hz with motion unchanged. Observed strong response at600 Hz; independently observed displacement antinodes at both ends. Infer received frequencies, compare candidates and verify conclusion.

A source/receiver travels away from a fixed wall at 15 m/s, initially 105 m away. Sound speed in stationary medium is315 m/s and source frequency300 Hz. Find first echo delay and reception distance; derive spacing of fronts emitted toward the wall (behind source), and reflected encounter frequency. A measured steady echo frequency is exactly270 Hz. Test the ideal account.
